query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Rapid thermal annealing (RTA) of an as-deposited, equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy will induce sufficient atomic rearrangement to form a lower-symmetry, chemically ordered phase (e.g., L10 ordering) or anisotropic lattice distortions that increase magnetocrystalline anisotropy via chemical short-range order, thereby significantly boosting the coercivity relative to the disordered fcc baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited, equiatomic, multicomponent FeCoNi high-entropy alloy with an fcc solid solution structure exhibiting high saturation magnetization but low coercivity.
generation.intervention: Apply rapid thermal annealing (RTA) under conditions that impart substrate-induced strain on Si/SiO2-supported thin films using brief high-temperature pulses.
generation.conditions: Thin film samples with a nearly equiatomic FeCoNi composition that satisfy the high configurational entropy requirement; RTA parameters (temperature and time) are chosen to promote ordering without triggering detrimental coarsening or phase separation, under the ambient conditions specified by the query.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a lower-symmetry, chemically ordered phase (such as L10) or anisotropic lattice distortions induced by the RTA process.
generation.mechanism: Rapid thermal annealing enhances atomic mobility and, through substrate-induced strain mediated by chemical short-range order, drives the transformation from a disordered fcc phase to an ordered (L10) or anisotropically distorted phase with reduced lattice symmetry, thereby increasing magnetocrystalline anisotropy and domain-wall pinning to boost coercivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The RTA-treated FeCoNi-based HEA will exhibit coercivity increased by up to one to three orders of magnitude over the as-deposited, disordered fcc state while largely retaining its high saturation magnetization.
generation.baseline: An unannealed or slowly cooled FeCoNi-based HEA in a chemically disordered fcc structure with inherently low coercivity.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected primarily in thin film samples processed under controlled RTA conditions; excessive annealing or use in bulk specimens may lead to unwanted phase separation or grain coarsening that could mitigate the coercivity enhancement.
generation.uncertainty: The exact RTA parameters (temperature, time, strain conditions) required to achieve the desired ordering and anisotropy are not fully determined; the degree of ordering and the resulting coercivity increase may vary based on processing specifics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of equiatomic FeCoNi HEA thin films on Si/SiO2 substrates and subject them to RTA at various temperatures and durations. Use X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy to determine if a lower-symmetry (e.g., L10) or anisotropically distorted phase has formed, and measure the magnetic hysteresis using vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM).
measurements: XRD patterns to detect phase transformations and evidence of chemical ordering (e.g., superlattice peaks characteristic of L10 ordering)
TEM for imaging lattice distortions and order
Magnetization hysteresis loops (via VSM) to quantify coercivity and saturation magnetization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the RTA-treated samples do not show any signatures of lower symmetry ordering or significant lattice distortion compared to the as-deposited baseline and if the measured coercivity does not increase by at least a factor of 10 over the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe vast high entropy alloy (HEA) composition space is promising for discovery of new material phases with unique properties. This study explores the potential to achieve rare‐earth‐free high magnetic anisotropy materials in single‐phase HEA thin films. Thin films of FeCoNiMnCu sputtered on thermally oxidized Si/SiO2 substrates at room temperature are magnetically soft, with a coercivity on the order of 10 Oe. After post‐deposition rapid thermal annealing (RTA), the films exhibit a single face‐centered‐cubic phase, with an almost 40‐fold increase in coercivity. Inclusion of 50 at.% Pt in the film leads to ordering of a single L10 high entropy intermetallic phase after RTA, along with high magnetic anisotropy and 3 orders of magnitude coercivity increase. These results demonstrate a promising HEA approach to achieve high magnetic anisotropy materials using RTA.Keywords: high entropy alloy, magnetic anisotropy, rapid thermal annealing High entropy alloy (HEA) thin films are explored to achieve high magnetic anisotropy phases. The 1–2 orders of magnitude coercivity increase in RTA‐treated samples, compared to the as‐grown ones, suggests the emergence of sizeable magnetic anisotropy in the film. The fact that the continuous 15s RTA sample (Figure 1b) exhibits a 350 Oe coercivity, indicates that the dewetting process and film morphology evolution in some of the samples are not essential to the significant coercivity enhancement. Previous studies on bulk FeCoNiMnCu solid solutions have not found appreciable magnetic anisotropy ascribed to the disordered phase.[ ,  ] Hard magnetic properties in some solid solutions have been attributed to the magnetocrystalline or shape anisotropy of a secondary phase, however, studies of bulk phase‐separated FeCoNiMnCu have not shown large coercivity of the order presented here.[  ] In the present RTA‐treated samples, likely the anisotropic strain has induced lattice and grain distortions or directional chemical order, different from those in bulk systems, and stabilized sizable magnetic anisotropy, similar to that in RTA‐assisted synthesis of L10 FeCuPt.[ ,  ]
